messages.subject: Understanding goodness-of-fit results
parts:
Hi all,

As I specified in a previous message, I am fairly new to the unmarked package and am trying to work through some problems.

I have a dataset that includes double observer data for a single date/ season. The data looks like this:
Species site ob1 ob2 ob1ID ob2ID
AMCR    A     1     1        Jane    John
AMCR    B      0     1       Jane    John
 . . . .
AMCR   Y       1    1          Fred    Barbara
AMCR   Z       0    0          Fred    Barbara


I have created global models for the individual species in the dataset using the occu() function, and have used the mb.gof.test() function

from the AICcmodavg package to perform goodness-of-fit tests. However, for a fair number of the species, the c-hat is greater than 4.

For example, for AMCR, the results are

   Cohort Observed Expected Chi-square
00      0      146   133.39       1.19
01      0       25    39.79       5.50
10      0       20    30.42       3.57
11      0       63    50.40       3.15


The results suggest that (1,1) and (0,0) occurs more often than expected, with (1,0) and (0,1) underrepresented. But the site data really aren't independent and it isn't unexpected that AMCR, if heard by one observer, would be heard by both observers. Since the c-hat is above 1 (8.2), the results suggest the data is overdispersed. In the MacKenzie and Bailey paper from 2004, an example is given where two sites are situated too close together and thus there is overcounting. In the current example, there is clearly overcounting!

I guess what I am asking is (1) using the mb.gof.test the appropriate way to analyze the dataset I have, and if not, what would be a better way?

messages.author: 4e956cc50ac3e075
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Understanding goodness-of-fit results
parts:
Hi Wade,

For a species that is easy to detect, it is more likely that both
observers will detect it during the same period. Are these two
observers independent and sampling simultaneously at the same site? Or
are they sampling at different times?

Some things that may help:
-add better covariates on detection and/or occupancy
-change the model (e.g., perhaps time to detection)
-change the data (e.g., work on guilds instead of species, exclude
species)

You indicate in your message that "the site data really aren't
independent". Do you mean that sites are close to one another and the
same individual can be detected at different sites? If there is a
spatial structure in your collection of sites (nested in region or
along a transect), then you could incorporate this structure in the
model.

Regardless, a c-hat of 8.2 indicates that you can't continue the
analysis with the current model for a given species (overdispersion is
much too high). Also be aware that although some species will be
amenable to a single species occupancy analysis, you cannot expect the
model to fit for every species (some species will too rare or common).
A multispecies model would be another option and could accommodate rare
or common species, although the approach would be outside of unmarked
(AHM1 book by Marc Kéry and Andy Royle is a good place to start).

Good luck,

Marc

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Understanding goodness-of-fit results
parts:
Hi Marc,

Thanks for reply.  When I wrote that the "sites really aren't independent", what I meant was that the observers were at the same site at the same time. In my limited understanding of occupancy modeling, the double observer ( two observers at the same site at the same time) and a case where a single observer went to the same site on two different occasions are modeled the same way, but do have some differences. As you stated in your reply, if a bird song is loud and close, it is more likely to be heard by both observers and thus an overabundance of (1,1) cases.

I am curios about everyone's thoughts about my solution. I "solved" my problem by randomizing the observations across each row. Since the data only has a single time (with two observers), cases can be (0,0), (1,0),(0,1), and (1,1). If (1,0) are different than (0,1), this can generate model fit errors (with c-hat above 4). However, if one randomizes across rows, the cases of (0,1) and (1,0) become roughly the same and c-hat decreases accordingly. This preserves the values (there are the same number of 0s and 1s).

I can't think of a reason why this would be a problem, but you all are smarter than I am, so just wanted to throw this out to see what people thought.
